title: PostgreSQL with Drizzle, MongoDB with Mongoose
summary: Define tables and migrations with Drizzle, keep queries and transactions safe in repositories, and use Mongoose models with pre-save hooks.
intro: The API bugs that cost real money live at the database: an oversold seat, a half-written order, a password stored in plain text. This lesson reads the data layer of two codebases, StagePass on PostgreSQL with Drizzle ORM and Cookbook on MongoDB with Mongoose. You will see where the schema lives, how changes reach the database, how writes stay correct when requests race, and how hooks run code before and after a write.

steps.title: Tables, migrations, and queries
steps.body:
With Drizzle, the schema is TypeScript. `src/db/schema.ts` declares every table with `pgTable`: its columns and its constraints. Two things come from it: the types your code uses, and the SQL migrations in `drizzle/`.

The workflow you will use on the job:

1. Change `src/db/schema.ts`.
2. Run `npm run db:generate`. drizzle-kit compares the schema with its last snapshot and writes a new SQL file.
3. Read that SQL, then run `npm run db:migrate` to apply it.

Never edit a migration that has already run somewhere. Add a new one instead.

Queries live in repositories and use Drizzle's SQL-shaped builder: `select`, `insert`, `update`, `delete`, `where`, joins, and the `sql` template for anything else. Every value goes to PostgreSQL as a parameter, never pasted into the SQL text, so input cannot change the query.

examples.title: A table and its rules
examples.prompt: `ticket_types` stores prices and seat counts. Look at the checks at the bottom.
examples.explanation: Columns are camelCase in TypeScript and snake_case in SQL, so `priceCents` is `price_cents`. Money is whole cents in an integer, never a float. The checks are the database's own rules, and they hold whatever the code above them does: `sold <= capacity` is the last line of defense against overselling. Deleting an event cascades to its ticket types.

examples.title: The generated migration
examples.prompt: `drizzle-kit generate` wrote this file from the table definition.
examples.code:
CREATE TABLE "ticket_types" (
	"id" integer PRIMARY KEY GENERATED BY DEFAULT AS IDENTITY (sequence name "ticket_types_id_seq" INCREMENT BY 1 MINVALUE 1 MAXVALUE 2147483647 START WITH 1 CACHE 1),
	"event_id" integer NOT NULL,
	"name" text NOT NULL,
	"price_cents" integer NOT NULL,
	"capacity" integer NOT NULL,
	"sold" integer DEFAULT 0 NOT NULL,
	"created_at" timestamp with time zone NOT NULL,
	"updated_at" timestamp with time zone NOT NULL,
	CONSTRAINT "ticket_types_event_id_name_unique" UNIQUE("event_id","name"),
	CONSTRAINT "ticket_types_price_check" CHECK ("ticket_types"."price_cents" >= 0),
	CONSTRAINT "ticket_types_capacity_check" CHECK ("ticket_types"."capacity" > 0),
	CONSTRAINT "ticket_types_sold_check" CHECK ("ticket_types"."sold" >= 0),
	CONSTRAINT "ticket_types_sold_within_capacity_check" CHECK ("ticket_types"."sold" <= "ticket_types"."capacity")
);
--> statement-breakpoint
ALTER TABLE "ticket_types" ADD CONSTRAINT "ticket_types_event_id_events_id_fk" FOREIGN KEY ("event_id") REFERENCES "public"."events"("id") ON DELETE cascade ON UPDATE no action;
examples.explanation: This is plain SQL that you read in code review, and it is exactly what runs in production. Each constraint keeps the name the schema gave it, so an error that names `ticket_types_sold_within_capacity_check` tells you which rule was broken. Drizzle records every migration it applies in its own table, so `db:migrate` only runs the files a database has not seen yet.

examples.title: A query with optional filters
examples.prompt: The public event list builds up to seven conditions. All but the first are optional.
examples.explanation: `and()` skips `undefined` entries, so each optional filter is one line. Values such as `query.city` are sent as parameters. The `sql` template covers what the builder lacks, here full text search with `websearch_to_tsquery`, and it still sends `query.q` as a parameter. Ordering by the sort column and then by `id` keeps the order stable when two events start at the same moment.

steps.title: Transactions and hooks with Drizzle
steps.body:
Some writes must happen together or not at all. A checkout reserves seats, inserts the order and its items, and writes an audit row. StagePass runs such work inside `withTx(db, fn)`, a wrapper around Drizzle's `db.transaction` that also retries when PostgreSQL aborts a transaction for a deadlock. Repository methods accept the transaction as their `db` argument, so the same query works inside or outside one.

A transaction alone does not stop races. If you read `sold`, compare it in JavaScript, and write it back, two buyers can both take the last seat. Use one atomic statement that checks and writes together.

Drizzle has no model hooks like Mongoose's `pre("save")`, so StagePass adds its own. A service calls `hooks.run(name, payload, tx)` just before or after a write, and other modules register functions for that name. The hooks get the same transaction, so their writes commit or roll back with the change.

examples.title: Reserve seats atomically
examples.prompt: This is how checkout takes seats, with no read before the write. The output is the answer to the `Sold out: 409` request in `requests.http`, which asks for one ticket of type 2, a VIP ticket that is sold out.
examples.explanation: The `WHERE` adds the quantity only if the result still fits the capacity. `UPDATE` takes a row lock, so a second buyer's update waits for the first to finish, then checks the condition again against the new `sold`. When no row matches, `reserve` returns `null`, the checkout service throws `SoldOutError`, and the whole transaction rolls back. `returning()` hands back the updated row, so the order charges the price the database holds right now.

examples.title: A write with a before hook
examples.prompt: Creating an event runs its hooks and the insert in one transaction.
examples.explanation: The service first checks the rules that need no lock: the start time and the venue. Inside `withTx`, `hooks.run("event.beforeCreate", ...)` lets every registered hook change the draft, and the insert uses the result. If no hook set a slug, the service throws, because a missing hook is a bug that should fail loudly. If anything throws inside `withTx`, PostgreSQL rolls back the whole transaction.

examples.title: The slug hook
examples.prompt: This module attaches behavior to event writes without `EventsService` knowing about it.
examples.explanation: Before an event is created, the hook trims the title and picks a free slug: `open-mic-night`, then `open-mic-night-2`. It checks with the same `tx` as the insert, so it sees the transaction's own writes. On an update, a draft's slug follows its title, but a published event keeps its slug, because people have already shared its link.

steps.title: Mongoose models and pre-save hooks
steps.body:
Mongoose gives MongoDB documents a schema: field types, validation, defaults, indexes, and **middleware hooks** that run before or after an operation. Cookbook keeps its data rules in the models, so they hold for every write.

The hook you will meet most is `pre("save")`. In Mongoose 9 a pre hook is an `async function` with no `next()`: return to continue, or throw to stop the save. Write it as a regular `function`, not an arrow function, because Mongoose passes the document as `this`.

Hooks belong to operations, and that is the classic trap. `save()` and `create()` run document hooks. `updateOne()` and `findOneAndUpdate()` send the update straight to MongoDB, so they skip `pre("save")` and, by default, validation. That is why Cookbook edits a recipe by loading it, calling `set()`, and saving it.

examples.title: Hash the password before saving
examples.prompt: Signup assigns the plain password to `user.password`. The hook replaces it with an argon2 hash before the document is written.
examples.explanation: `isModified("password")` is the line that matters. Without it, saving a user after a name change would hash the stored hash, and that user could never log in again. `select: false` keeps the hash out of normal queries, so login must ask for it with `.select("+password")`. The schema also cleans and checks emails: they are trimmed, lowercased, and matched against a pattern.

examples.title: Load, set, save
examples.prompt: This is how Cookbook edits a recipe, so its hooks and validators run.
examples.explanation: `findOne` loads the document, the service checks that the caller is the author, and `recipe.set(changes)` applies the validated fields. `save()` then runs the `pre("validate")` hook, which picks a new unique slug when the title changed, and the schema's validators. A `findOneAndUpdate` here would save a round trip and silently skip both.

examples.title: Hooks after a write
examples.prompt: Post hooks run after the write. Cookbook uses them to keep each recipe's rating correct.
examples.explanation: After a review is saved, `calcRatings` recomputes the recipe's `ratingAvg` and `ratingCount` from all of its reviews. Recomputing from scratch is safe to run twice, which matters because the write has already happened. The delete hook is registered for `findOneAndDelete` only. `Review.deleteOne()` would run no hook and leave the rating stale, so the reviews service deletes with `findOneAndDelete` on purpose.

recap:
- With Drizzle the schema is TypeScript: generate a SQL migration from it, read it, then apply it. Never edit a migration that already ran.
- Keep every query in a repository, and send every value as a parameter.
- Put writes that belong together in one transaction, and replace read-then-write with one atomic `UPDATE ... WHERE`.
- Let constraints such as `CHECK (sold <= capacity)` be the last line of defense.
- Mongoose `pre("save")` hooks run on `save()` and `create()`, not on `updateOne()` or `findOneAndUpdate()`. Guard them with `isModified()`.
